title: TikTok and prostate cancer: misinformation and quality of information using validated questionnaires
screen_reason: Census content analysis of all 65 TikTok videos carrying #prostatecancer between 12 June 2016 and 30 June 2020 (55 analysed after excluding 7 private and 3 non-English). Two coders with prostate-cancer expertise scored each video for misinformation on a published 5-point Likert scale (inter-rater reliability 99.6%) and the paper reports 'Among 17 videos (totaling 95285 views) with objective information, 7 (41%, 3795 views) had a significant amount of misinformation' - a CONTENT falsity share with an explicit denominator. DISCERN quality results are additionally reported and are kept as a QUALITY row only.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language TikTok videos worldwide (authors in the United States)
estimates.date: 12 June 2016 to 30 June 2020 (all videos published in this window)
estimates.measure_type: % of informational #prostatecancer TikTok videos containing a significant amount of misinformation
estimates.value_raw: Among 17 videos (totaling 95285 views) with objective information, 7 (41%, 3795 views) had a significant amount of misinformation
estimates.denominator: 17 TikTok videos judged to contain objective information (out of 55 #prostatecancer videos analysed; 65 identified, 7 private and 3 non-English excluded)
estimates.definition: A video counted for the numerator if two expert coders scored it as having a significant amount of misinformation on a published 5-point Likert misinformation scale; examples given are promoting routine PSA screening beginning at age 30 and promoting a 'miracle cure' beverage
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; misinformation operationalised by "a published 5-point Likert scale" applied by prostate-cancer experts, with exemplars of clinically incorrect advice ("promoting routine PSA screening beginning at age 30, promoting a “miracle cure” beverage")
estimates.source_quote: Among 17 videos (totaling 95285 views) with objective information, 7 (41%, 3795 views) had a significant amount of misinformation (e.g., promoting routine PSA screening beginning at age 30, promoting a “miracle cure” beverage).
estimates.page_loc: Results (research communication, unpaginated accepted version), paragraph beginning 'The median expert-rated quality of videos was 2/5 on DISCERN'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers with prostate-cancer (CaP) expertise scored every video; misinformation scored with a published 5-point Likert scale (Struck et al. 2018); inter-rater reliability reported as 99.6% (percentage agreement, no kappa).
estimates.moderator_quote: We reviewed all TikTok videos (n=65) with the hashtag #prostatecancer between 6/12/16 and 6/30/20. Ten were excluded (7 private and 3 non-English), leaving 55 for analysis. ... Videos were also scored for the presence of misinformation, using a published 5-point Likert scale.[4] ... Inter-rater reliability was 99.6% between two coders with PCa expertise.
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT denominator caveat: the base is not all 55 videos but the 17 that carried objective information (the other 38 were awareness posts, patient stories, etc. with no substantive claims to assess). Hence denom_selection=curated even though the hashtag itself was censused (all 65 videos in the window were retrieved, no rank truncation - sampling_frame=full_census). Expressed over the whole corpus the figure would be 7/55 = 12.7%, but that is a computed share against a different denominator and is not kept per R8.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language TikTok videos worldwide (authors in the United States)
estimates.measure_type: % of #prostatecancer TikTok videos rated moderate to poor quality on DISCERN
estimates.value_raw: Fifty-four (98.2%) videos were moderate to poor quality, accounting for 134752 or 97.4% of total views
estimates.definition: A video counted for the numerator if its expert-rated DISCERN score placed it in the moderate-to-poor quality band (median DISCERN score across videos was 2/5)
estimates.misinfo_def: Not a falsity measure: DISCERN is a 16-item quality-criteria instrument for consumer health information, scored 1 = poor to 5 = excellent
estimates.source_quote: The median expert-rated quality of videos was 2/5 on DISCERN. Fifty-four (98.2%) videos were moderate to poor quality, accounting for 134752 or 97.4% of total views.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers with prostate-cancer expertise applied the 16-item DISCERN instrument (1 = poor to 5 = excellent); inter-rater reliability 99.6%.
estimates.moderator_quote: Videos were examined using 2 validated instruments: DISCERN quality criteria for consumer health information with 16 items ranked from 1=poor to 5=excellent,[6] and the Patient Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) with 17 items evaluating understandability and actionability.
estimates.notes: QUALITY, not prevalence: most of these videos are awareness posts and patient tributes that make no factual claims at all, so a low DISCERN score says nothing about falsity. Kept for the appendix. The same sentence also gives a view-weighted version (97.4% of 134,944 views went to moderate-to-poor-quality videos), which is a second verbatim share of the same construct on a views denominator; not rowed separately per R4.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The view-weighted quality figure (134,752 views, 97.4% of total views, on moderate-to-poor-quality videos) is verbatim and could be a separate QUALITY row with a views denominator; folded into the QUALITY row's notes instead. 2) The misinformation videos' views (3,795 of 95,285 views on informational videos = 4.0%) would be an exposure-weighted misinformation share, but the percentage is not printed and would have to be computed, so it is excluded by R8. 3) 7/55 = 12.7% over the full corpus is likewise a computed re-basing and was not kept. 4) 'Six (10.1%) videos had apparent commercial bias (e.g. advertising incontinence pads), with 1156 (0.83%) total views' - commercial bias, not falsity, so not extracted (note also that 6/55 = 10.9%, not 10.1%, an apparent slip in the paper). 5) PEMAT understandability (median 75%) and actionability (median 0%) are scale scores, not shares of items. 6) Content-type shares (awareness 30%, patient story 29%, informational 14%, complementary/alternative medicine 6%, new technology 6%) and publisher demographics are topic/source categories, not falsity. 7) The Introduction refers to the authors' earlier YouTube study of misinformative prostate-cancer content; no figure is quoted and it would be excluded by R8 anyway.

rob.design: Cross-sectional census content analysis. Frame: all TikTok videos carrying the hashtag #prostatecancer published between 12 June 2016 and 30 June 2020 (n = 65); 10 excluded (7 private, 3 non-English), 55 analysed, 134,944 total views, 53 unique publishers. Coding: two independent reviewers with prostate-cancer expertise annotated objective metadata, topic, target audience, perceived publisher demographics and comments, and scored each video with DISCERN (16 items), PEMAT (17 items) and a published 5-point Likert misinformation scale. Reliability: inter-rater agreement 99.6% (percentage agreement between the two coders; no kappa, no adjudication procedure described). Very small sample; the misinformation estimate rests on 7 events in 17 videos, so its precision is poor and no confidence interval is given. Authors note that instruments designed for longer patient-education material fit short-form TikTok content badly (e.g. only 14 videos had any call to action).
